stops.name: Kibamba, Lake Tanganyika, the crossing to Africa
stops.campa: By night launch across Lake Tanganyika, Tatu lands at the rebel base of Kibamba under the Congolese mountains: the first and only time Che Guevara opens a front in person on a new continent. He finds an army that fires from the hip with eyes closed, commanders absent in the bars of Kigoma, and a magic called dawa painted on the fighters to turn bullets to water; he records the belief without mockery and works within it, drilling, doctoring, teaching. He asks to fight as a simple soldier until merit earns him command. The mountains hold seven months of his life.

stops.name: Front de Force / Bendera, the defeat at the power station
stops.campa: Against his judgment but under orders from the distant rebel leadership, the attack goes in against the fortified hydroelectric garrison at Front de Force-Bendera. It fails bloodily; four Cubans die, and in a dead man's pocket the enemy finds a diary that tells Pretoria, Langley and the world that Cubans are fighting in the Congo. The Simbas blame the failure of the dawa and drift away from the front. Che, sick with fevers and asthma in the wet mountains, writes the post-mortem with his customary refusal of consolation: the revolution cannot be imported into an army that will not fight.

stops.name: Lake Tanganyika, the evacuation, 'the history of a failure'
stops.campa: Mobutu's coup, mercenary columns, gunboats on the lake: the eastern rebellion collapses, and on the night of the twenty-first of November the Cubans are taken off the beach at Kibamba in overloaded boats, Che boarding among the last, arguing to the final hour about staying behind alone. Crossing the black water back to Tanzania he begins, in his head, the merciless book of the campaign. Its first sentence, already composed, will open with defeat declared like a diagnosis. The canon values the Congo above many victories, because here the myth proves it can tell the truth about itself.
stops.quote: This is the history of a failure.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, Congo Diary, opening line, written up in Dar es Salaam, late 1965

stops.name: Prague, the ghost year
stops.campa: The man who renounced his citizenships now belongs to no country at all. After months hidden in the upper room of the Cuban embassy in Dar es Salaam, writing the Congo book, receiving Aleida in secret for a stolen honeymoon of exiles, he moves to a safe house outside Prague under Czech winter skies, disguised, restless, studying philosophy and the maps of Bolivia. Fidel writes urging him back to Cuba to prepare the next war properly. The canon calls this the ghost year: the world debates whether Che is dead, while he drills his own resurrection.

stops.name: La Paz, Hotel Copacabana, the bald economist
stops.campa: Adolfo Mena González, balding, bespectacled, middle-aged economist of the Organization of American States, checks into room 504 of the Hotel Copacabana on the Prado of La Paz. In the mirror of the wardrobe he photographs himself, pipe in hand: the famous self-portrait of the disguise. Thirteen years after he watched the half-made Bolivian revolution as a hitchhiking doctor, Che re-enters Bolivia to finish the continent's business: a guerrilla foco to draw the Yankees in and make, as he will write, two, three, many Vietnams. Nobody looks twice at the quiet gentleman by the window.

stops.name: Ñancahuazú, the Casa de Calamina, 'a new stage begins'
stops.campa: By jeep across the altiplano and down into the scrub canyons of the southeast, he reaches the farm bought as a front on the Ñancahuazú river: the tin-roofed Casa de Calamina. That night, by lamplight, he rules a fresh notebook and writes the first entry of the last diary: today begins a new stage. Around him gather the fifty of the ELN: Cuban comandantes of the Sierra, Bolivian miners, the woman Tania come down from her deep cover in La Paz society, Régis Debray the French philosopher, Ciro Bustos the Argentine painter. The canyon country will be their monastery, then their trap.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, The Bolivian Diary, first entry, 7 November 1966

stops.name: The Río Grande, the training march and the first deaths
stops.campa: In February the column leaves camp for a training march meant to last two weeks; the country itself declares war instead. For forty-eight days they hack through canyons and thorn, rivers in flood, rations gone, men eating parrots and palm hearts. At the swollen Río Grande the young Bolivian Benjamín, weak with exhaustion, slips from the rocks and the current takes him, the guerrilla's first death, given not by the army but by the land. Days later the river drowns Carlos at another crossing. Che records the omens exactly, and marches the survivors home to find the camp already betrayed.

stops.name: Ñancahuazú river, the first ambush, 23 March
stops.campa: Deserters have talked; the army comes probing up the canyon. The guerrilla's ambush along the Ñancahuazú kills seven soldiers and takes prisoners, weapons and the army's operational plans in the war's opening minutes. The diary entry begins with the day's plain designation: a day of warlike events. The war has started five months early, with the network unbuilt, Debray and Bustos trapped as guests, and the Bolivian Communist Party withholding its men. Che knows the arithmetic and fights anyway; from this day the column is in continuous motion until the ravine at the end.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, The Bolivian Diary, 23 March 1967

stops.name: Iripití, the double ambush, the death of El Rubio
stops.campa: At Iripití on the tenth of April the guerrilla springs the same ambush twice in one day, mauling two army companies, taking scores of prisoners and a harvest of weapons, tactically the campaign's most brilliant day. Its price: Captain Jesús Suárez Gayol, El Rubio, veteran of the Sierra and vice-minister in Havana who left a ministry desk for this canyon, lies dead by the river, shot through the head, his grenade unthrown beside him. The diary honors him as the first Cuban blood in Bolivia. Victory and loss are entered in the same column now, every week.

stops.name: Muyupampa, Debray and Bustos walk out
stops.campa: To free the column of its civilians, Che maneuvers to the town of Muyupampa so that Debray and Bustos can slip out disguised as journalists. They are taken within hours, beaten, and paraded; the world learns from their capture that Che Guevara lives and commands in Bolivia. The Yankees respond in kind: Green Berets arrive to raise a Ranger battalion, and the CIA seconds its Cuban-exile interrogators. Worse, in the maneuvering the column splits from Joaquín's rearguard, seventeen men including Tania, and the two halves of the guerrilla will search for each other through the canyons for four months, never to meet again.

stops.name: On the march near the Río Rosita, the thirty-ninth birthday
stops.campa: Deep in the campaign's wandering middle, no radio contact with Havana, no peasant recruits, asthma returning because the medicines were lost with the caves, Che turns thirty-nine on the trail and marks the day in the diary with one of its rare personal entries, measuring himself against the age when a guerrilla must begin to consider his future. The column eats horse meat and moves. The tone is neither hope nor despair but inventory: he is still whole, still fit for the work. The canon reads the entry as the last calm self-portrait, taken standing, in motion, armed.
stops.quote: I have reached thirty-nine and the age is inexorably approaching when I must consider my future as a guerrilla; for now, I am still 'whole'.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, The Bolivian Diary, 14 June 1967

stops.name: Samaipata, the raid on the highway town
stops.campa: In the campaign's boldest stroke, the guerrillas flag down vehicles on the Santa Cruz highway, drive into the garrison town of Samaipata by night, seize the post, empty the pharmacy and the shops before the astonished townspeople, and vanish back into the hills with prisoners taken and released. It is the war's greatest propaganda victory and its emptiest: the pharmacy holds none of the asthma medicine Che now needs to breathe. The army encircles the zone with thousands. The foco is famous across the world's front pages, and utterly alone in its canyons.
